opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the geometric view is one of the most useful mental tools we have, because a lot of what a transformer does is move information around in a shared space. You've got this residual stream, a big high-dimensional vector at every token position, and every layer reads from it and writes back into it. Once you see it that way, a lot of questions about composition become questions about directions and dot products.

The basic intuition is that a feature, some concept the model represents, like "this token is part of a city name" or "we're inside a quotation," corresponds roughly to a direction in that space. When a later component wants to use that information, it effectively takes a dot product with that direction. It projects the residual stream onto the thing it cares about. If the vector points strongly that way, the downstream component "sees" the feature. If it's orthogonal, it doesn't.

That gives you a clean way to think about how computations chain together. Say an early layer writes a feature into the residual stream, and a later attention head or MLP neuron reads it. Whether that connection actually exists comes down to whether the write direction and the read direction line up. So you can ask, for any two components, how much does the output of this one project onto the input of that one? That's essentially what you're measuring when you build attribution graphs or look at virtual weights between features in different layers. You're tracing which writes land on which reads.

Where it gets interesting, and a bit messy, is superposition. The model wants to represent far more features than it has dimensions, so features can't all be orthogonal. They're packed in at angles that are nearly orthogonal but not quite. That means when a downstream component projects onto one feature, it picks up a little interference from others that are close by. The geometry tells you where to expect that crosstalk. And it explains why the model often seems to rely on sparsity. If only a few features are active at once, the interference stays manageable, even though the directions overlap.

So in practice, when I'm trying to understand a circuit, say how a model does a multi-step reasoning thing like "the capital of the state containing Dallas," I'm thinking about it as a sequence of these projections. Some feature for "Dallas" gets written, something reads it and writes a "Texas" representation, and then something downstream reads the "Texas" direction combined with "capital" and writes toward "Austin." Each step is a read-and-write in that geometric space, and the question at every hop is whether the directions actually connect.

It's not a perfect picture. Nonlinearities, attention patterns, and layer norm all complicate the pure linear story. But as a first-order way of reasoning about composition, thinking in terms of directions, alignment, and projection gets you surprisingly far, and it gives you hypotheses you can actually test by intervening on those directions and seeing whether the downstream behavior changes the way you'd predict.

r001.rationale: The response describes an early layer writing along a direction and a later component reading it through a dot product, then frames composition as tracing how those write and read directions align across successive steps.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I like to think about it is that pretty much everything happening inside a transformer is linear algebra in a shared space, and the two operations that matter most are "how aligned are these two vectors" and "what does this vector look like when you project it onto some direction." Once you've internalized that, a lot of the mystery about how computations chain together goes away.

So take the residual stream. Every layer reads from it and writes back into it, and the thing it writes is just added. There's no overwriting, it's additive. That means the residual stream at any point is a sum of contributions from the embedding, from every attention head, from every MLP neuron that fired before. If a head writes out some direction, say the direction that encodes "the subject of this sentence is plural," then any later component can pick up on that information by having a read weight that has a large dot product with that direction. The later component doesn't need to know where that information came from. It just projects the residual stream onto its input direction, and if the plural feature was written in, the projection is large and it activates.

And that's really the whole mechanism of composition. One component writes a vector, another component reads along a direction, and the amount of signal that gets through is the cosine similarity between them scaled by the magnitude. If the output direction of component A and the input direction of component B are nearly orthogonal, they basically can't talk to each other, no matter what else is going on. If they're well aligned, you've got a wire connecting them. So you can take a pair of weights, say the output weights of one neuron and the input weights of another, multiply them together, and that product tells you directly how much the first one can influence the second. We do this all the time when we're tracing circuits. You don't need to run the model to know that two features are connected, you can read it off the geometry.

Where it gets more interesting is when you go from neurons to features. Models represent far more features than they have dimensions, so features aren't orthogonal, they're packed in at small angles to each other. That means when a component writes feature X, it also leaks a little bit onto every feature that's nearby in angle. Most of the time that interference is small enough to be ignored, but it's exactly the kind of thing that shows up as weird behavior, where a feature that has nothing to do with the task gets partially activated because it happens to share some direction with one that does.

Attention fits into the same picture. The query and key projections are just asking, for every pair of positions, how similar are these two vectors after I project them onto the subspace this head cares about. The head isn't looking at the full residual stream, it's looking at a low-rank slice of it. So the question "will this head attend to that token" becomes "do the write directions of earlier components land in the subspace this head's QK circuit is reading, and do they land in a way that makes query and key align." And then the OV circuit is another projection and write, moving some subspace of the attended token's residual into the current position.

So if you ask me how a multi-step computation happens, the honest answer is it's a chain of these. Something gets written into a direction. Something downstream has a read direction that overlaps with it, so it fires, does its little nonlinear thing, and writes a new direction. Something further downstream reads that. And at each step, the strength of the link is literally a dot product you can compute. That's why I find the geometric framing so useful. It takes composition, which sounds abstract, and turns it into something you can measure between any two parts of the network.

r001.rationale: The response describes an earlier component writing a direction and a later component reading the accumulated signal by projecting onto its input direction, with the link strength determined by alignment or a dot product. It presents these successive geometric operations as the basis of composition.

astra-6.text:
I think the geometric view gives you a useful way to think about what one part of a model is writing and what another part is reading. A vector has a direction and a magnitude, and a dot product tells you how much of that vector lies along a particular direction. So you can think of a computation as asking, “How much of the thing I care about is present here?”

Then, to understand how computations compose, you look at whether the output of one computation points in a direction that a later computation is sensitive to. If those directions align, the first computation can strongly affect the second. If they’re orthogonal, that particular output won’t affect that particular readout.

For a simple linear example, suppose one operation writes a vector v, and a later operation reads using a vector w. The contribution to that readout is proportional to the dot product of w and v. That gives you a concrete way to reason about the connection between the two operations.

Of course, a model also has nonlinearities and computations that depend on the input, so a single alignment doesn’t explain everything. But it gives you a starting point: what information is being written, which directions carry it, and which later computations can pick it up?

r001.rationale: The response explains that an earlier operation writes vector v and a later operation reads using vector w, with the later readout depending on their dot product. This communicates how the earlier direction’s contribution composes with a later similarity computation.

sol-6.1.text:
I like to think of a vector as representing a collection of features, and then a direction as a particular feature you might care about. Taking a dot product asks, roughly, how much of this vector points in that direction? A projection lets you isolate that component.

Then you can think about a model as composing operations on those representations. One computation might detect a feature and write its result into a particular direction. A later computation can read that direction, combine it with other information, and produce something else. So the interesting question becomes: does the output of one computation line up with what the next computation is looking for?

That gives you a way to reason about how individually simple operations can work together to produce more complex behavior. But you have to be careful: a direction doesn’t necessarily correspond to one clean, human-readable concept. The geometry is a useful way to investigate what’s happening, rather than a guarantee that we already understand it.

r001.rationale: The response describes projecting onto a direction and asks whether one computation’s output lines up with what the next seeks, but it does not clearly specify a later similarity computation against another direction.
